rationale: The four studies differ a lot in depth, 16S region and protocol, and their case/control ratios differ too. A random forest on pooled raw relative abundances can learn "which study is this" signals that only fake disease signal. This change keeps the genus-level random forest but makes each genus a centered log-ratio (CLR) value and then z-scores it within each study. That removes study-level shifts so the trees split on within-study case-vs-control differences, which is what the metric scores.

I'm adding alpha-diversity features to the per-study z-scored genus CLR. IBD consistently shows lower gut diversity, and the genus CLR values can't express that directly. The new features are OTU-level Shannon, inverse Simpson, genus-level Shannon, and expected richness at a fixed depth per study, computed analytically rather than by random subsampling so it stays deterministic. Like the genus features, each is z-scored within its study so differences in sequencing depth and protocol between studies don't leak in.

I'm adding family-level and phylum-level CLR features alongside the genus CLR, built from the same pseudocount, 2% prevalence filter and within-study z-scoring. IBD dysbiosis shows up most consistently at broad levels (loss of Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae, gain of Enterobacteriaceae, Proteobacteria vs Firmicutes). Family names are also assigned more consistently than genus names across studies with different 16S regions, since many reads end up in an unassigned `g__` bin, so these features should be less noisy and carry over better between studies.

I'm adding a few features built from known IBD marker taxa: the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index plus two log-ratio summaries (butyrate producers vs Enterobacteriaceae, Proteobacteria vs Firmicutes). The dysbiosis index is the log ratio of IBD-enriched families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae) to depleted orders (Erysipelotrichales, Bacteroidales, Clostridiales). Each summary pools many weak, sparse taxa into one strong, label-free signal, which the forest can't easily rebuild from single CLR columns at random feature subsets. Like the other features, they are z-scored within each study.

I'm averaging the random forest with an L2 logistic regression on the same per-study z-scored features. The CLR and log-ratio features are compositional, and IBD dysbiosis is a broad shift spread across many taxa, which an additive linear model captures more smoothly and with less variance than trees. The regularization strength is picked by inner CV grouped by subject, and the two models are combined by averaging their ranks so their different probability scales don't matter.

IBD dysbiosis is a move away from the healthy "core" community (Halfvarson 2017: IBD samples drift outside the healthy plateau). Within each study I measure how atypical each sample is: Bray-Curtis distance to the study's median genus profile, mean Bray-Curtis distance to all other samples in the study, and Aitchison (CLR) distance to the study's mean genus and family profiles. These use no labels, are computed separately per study, and are z-scored within study. This adds a beta-diversity "dysbiosis magnitude" signal that the per-taxon features can't express.

The four studies differ a lot in size (RISK dominates) and in case/control ratio, but scoring is within each study. So I'm giving every (study, class) cell the same total weight when fitting both the random forest and the logistic regression. Then the smaller studies' case-vs-control patterns count as much as RISK's, and neither model can learn study-specific base rates. I haven't run this yet, so it has no Dev score so far.

I'm adding order-level and class-level CLR features (lineage prefixes up to `o__` and `c__`). Adding coarser levels gave the biggest gain so far (family and phylum, +0.031). Several key IBD signals are defined at order or class level: the Gevers dysbiosis index uses Clostridiales, Bacteroidales and Erysipelotrichales, plus Enterobacteriales and Gammaproteobacteria vs Clostridia. These names are assigned almost completely and consistently across the four studies' 16S regions. The new features use the same pseudocount, prevalence filter and within-study z-scoring as the existing levels. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'm adding a shallow, strongly regularized LightGBM as a third model in the rank-average, trained with the same balanced (study, class) weights. IBD dysbiosis looks threshold-like and interactive (an Enterobacteriaceae/Proteobacteria bloom matters most once butyrate producers and diversity are already low). Boosting can fit those conditional effects more directly than the random forest's random-subset splits, and the L2 linear model can't fit them at all, so it should add useful diversity to the ensemble. This hasn't been run yet, so it has no Dev score.

I'm replacing the within-study z-score with a within-study rank-based inverse-normal transform. The four studies differ in more than mean and spread: zero-inflation, depth and 16S region change the whole shape of each feature's distribution, which a z-score can't fix. Matching full distributions should make each study's case-vs-control contrasts comparable, both for the pooled trees and for the linear model, which outliers would otherwise dominate. The transform stays label-free, and the features and models are otherwise unchanged.

I'm adding depth-harmonized genus presence features: for each genus, the analytically expected probability that it would still be detected if the sample were rarefied to a common per-study depth, z-scored within study. Gevers 2014 and others describe IBD as a loss of taxa (genera dropping out). The current CLR features blur that, because their pseudocount ties "absent" to sequencing depth. These presence features keep the run deterministic, since there is no random subsampling. Untested: there's no Dev score yet.

I'm changing how genus features are built: genera are now grouped by their full lineage up to genus (`k__…;f__X;g__Y`) instead of by the bare `g__` name. With the bare name, every unassigned genus (`g__` with an empty name) from every family gets pooled into one mixed bin. That bin holds a large share of reads, and its size depends on the study's 16S region, so it mixes IBD-depleted Lachnospiraceae/Ruminococcaceae with IBD-enriched Enterobacteriaceae. Splitting it by family turns study-dependent noise into family-specific features that matter biologically, and also changes the CLR geometric mean and genus Shannon.

The curated marker log-ratios gave a large gain in round 4 (+0.015), so this round expands that panel with more well-replicated IBD signatures that the per-taxon CLR columns spread too thin. These are: oral-origin taxa found in the gut (Veillonella, Haemophilus, Streptococcus, Fusobacterium, Gemella, Rothia and others; Gevers 2014) versus a core of health-associated taxa (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Christensenellaceae, Oscillospira, Coprococcus, Akkermansia), the Ruminococcus gnavus vs Faecalibacterium ratio, and the log relative abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. Each new feature pools many sparse taxa into one label-free score and is z-scored within study like the rest.

Right now the LR's C is picked by pooled inner-CV AUROC and the RF/LR blend weight is fixed at 0.5. The task is scored within study, and the studies have different case/control ratios, so pooled AUROC is the wrong selection target. This change uses one grouped inner CV that produces out-of-fold RF and LR predictions. It picks C and the blend weight by mean within-study AUROC, so model selection matches the metric. I haven't run it, so it has no Dev score yet.

Taxa are currently kept if they reach 2% prevalence in the pooled data, so a genus or family that only one study's 16S region/pipeline detects (often RISK-specific) survives. It then becomes a noisy feature that is constant in the other studies. Rounds 8 and 13 showed that adding features hurt, so I'm tightening the filter in a label-free, cross-study way: a taxon must also reach at least 5% prevalence within at least half of the studies. This keeps the features to taxa that are measured consistently across studies, which should give both the forest and the logistic regression a cleaner signal that carries over between studies.

Within-study z-scoring only partly removes study effects: the 16S region and depth still move the exact split values a random forest learns. I'm making the tree half of the ensemble an even rank-average of the current random forest and an ExtraTrees forest with the same features and weights. ExtraTrees picks split thresholds at random, so it should rely less on study-specific cut-points and smooth over the noisy, zero-inflated CLR features. The LR half stays at 50% weight, unchanged. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

Right now each study's features are centered on all of that study's samples, so the centre moves with the study's case/control ratio. In a case-heavy study the cases look less extreme than in a control-heavy one, which distorts the pooled models. This round I add a step in `fit_predict` that re-centres every study on the mean of its own training-fold controls, for both train and test samples, using training labels only. Every study then measures dysbiosis from the same healthy reference, an idea borrowed from control-referenced batch correction (Gibbons 2018). I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

Within-study AUROC depends only on how samples rank inside each study, but the RF, ET and LR scores are currently rank-normalized over the whole pooled test fold before being blended. So in a study where one model's scores are tightly bunched, the model with the wider spread effectively decides the blend there. This change rank-normalizes each component's scores within each test study before averaging, so every model gets its intended weight inside every study. Study labels are used only for this harmonization and never as a predictor.

The current pseudocount is half the smallest nonzero relative abundance, which is about 0.5/depth for each sample. So a zero becomes log(0.5/depth), and deep and shallow samples in the same study get very different values for an absent taxon. Most genera are zero in most samples, so this per-sample depth effect also moves the CLR geometric mean, and with it every present taxon's value. This change uses one fixed pseudocount per study (0.5 / median read depth of that study) for every CLR level, so absent taxa get the same value within a study and the depth artifact is removed from all compositional features. The within-study z-score still handles the remaining differences between studies.

Round 19 helped by giving every CLR level one fixed pseudocount per study (0.5 / study median depth). The marker log-ratios still use a raw 0.5-read pseudocount, so a missing marker group (often Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae or Fusobacteriaceae) is scored as log(0.5/depth) and reflects each sample's sequencing depth. This change builds the four marker features from relative abundances with that same per-study pseudocount, so an absent marker gets the same value for every sample in a study. The depth artifact should then drop out of these strongly predictive features.
